cases.prompt: Which of the four large trials of a DOAC against warfarin in atrial fibrillation (RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE, ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48) showed superiority over warfarin on stroke or systemic embolism, and which showed only non-inferiority?

keyPoints.text: RE-LY: dabigatran 110 mg was non-inferior to warfarin (relative risk 0.91), while dabigatran 150 mg was superior (relative risk 0.66, P<0.001 for superiority).

support.quote: 1.53% per year in the group that received 110 mg of dabigatran (relative risk with dabigatran, 0.91; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 1.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority)
1.11% per year in the group that received 150 mg of dabigatran (relative risk, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.82; P<0.001 for superiority)

keyPoints.text: ROCKET AF: rivaroxaban was non-inferior to warfarin; in the intention-to-treat analysis superiority was not shown (hazard ratio 0.88, P=0.12 for superiority).

support.quote: the primary end point occurred in 269 patients in the rivaroxaban group (2.1% per year) and in 306 patients in the warfarin group (2.4% per year) (hazard ratio, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.03; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P=0.12 for superiority)

keyPoints.text: ARISTOTLE: apixaban was superior to warfarin on stroke or systemic embolism (hazard ratio 0.79, P=0.01 for superiority).

support.quote: hazard ratio with apixaban, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 0.95; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P=0.01 for superiority

keyPoints.text: ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48: both edoxaban regimens were non-inferior to warfarin (high dose hazard ratio 0.79, low dose 1.07); in the intention-to-treat analysis high-dose edoxaban showed only a trend (hazard ratio 0.87, P=0.08).

support.quote: 1.18% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.79; 97.5% confidence interval [CI], 0.63 to 0.99; P<0.001 for noninferiority) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 1.07; 97.5% CI, 0.87 to 1.31; P=0.005 for noninferiority)
there was a trend favoring high-dose edoxaban versus warfarin (hazard ratio, 0.87; 97.5% CI, 0.73 to 1.04; P=0.08)

cases.rubric: Score each reference key point against the preserved original abstract; unsupported clinical conclusions score zero.

cases.prompt: How did major bleeding with each of the four pivotal DOAC regimens compare with warfarin in RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48?

keyPoints.text: RE-LY: major bleeding was lower with dabigatran 110 mg than with warfarin (2.71% vs 3.36% per year) but similar with 150 mg (3.11% per year, P=0.31).

support.quote: The rate of major bleeding was 3.36% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 2.71% per year in the group receiving 110 mg of dabigatran (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year in the group receiving 150 mg of dabigatran (P=0.31).

keyPoints.text: ROCKET AF: no significant difference between rivaroxaban and warfarin in major bleeding (major and non-major clinically relevant bleeding 14.9% vs 14.5% per year, hazard ratio 1.03).

support.quote: There was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding

Major and nonmajor clinically relevant bleeding occurred in 1475 patients in the rivaroxaban group (14.9% per year) and in 1449 in the warfarin group (14.5% per year) (hazard ratio, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.96 to 1.11; P=0.44)

keyPoints.text: ARISTOTLE: major bleeding was lower with apixaban than with warfarin (2.13% vs 3.09% per year, hazard ratio 0.69).

support.quote: The rate of major bleeding was 2.13% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 3.09% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001)

keyPoints.text: ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48: major bleeding was lower with both edoxaban doses than with warfarin (3.43% on warfarin vs 2.75% on high dose, hazard ratio 0.80, and 1.61% on low dose, hazard ratio 0.47).

support.quote: The annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)

cases.rubric: Score each reference key point against the preserved original abstract; unsupported clinical conclusions score zero.

cases.prompt: What does the meta-analysis of the four pivotal DOAC trials conclude about haemorrhagic stroke, mortality, intracranial and gastrointestinal bleeding versus warfarin, and are its haemorrhagic stroke findings consistent with what RE-LY and ARISTOTLE reported on their own?

keyPoints.text: The meta-analysis found that DOACs reduced stroke or systemic embolism by 19% (RR 0.81) compared with warfarin, mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (RR 0.49).

support.quote: New oral anticoagulants significantly reduced stroke or systemic embolic events by 19% compared with warfarin (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73-0·91; p<0·0001), mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38-0·64; p<0·0001)

keyPoints.text: The meta-analysis found reduced all-cause mortality (RR 0.90) and intracranial haemorrhage (RR 0.48) but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (RR 1.25) with DOACs.

support.quote: New oral anticoagulants also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85-0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39-0·59; p<0·0001), but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01-1·55; p=0·04)

keyPoints.text: ARISTOTLE individually reported fewer haemorrhagic strokes with apixaban than warfarin (0.24% vs 0.47% per year, hazard ratio 0.51).

support.quote: The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.24% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 0.47% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.35 to 0.75; P<0.001)

keyPoints.text: RE-LY individually reported fewer haemorrhagic strokes with both dabigatran doses than with warfarin (0.12% and 0.10% vs 0.38% per year).

support.quote: The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.38% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 0.12% per year with 110 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001) and 0.10% per year with 150 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001).

cases.rubric: Score each reference key point against the preserved original abstract; unsupported clinical conclusions score zero.

cases.prompt: What did the evidence show about low-dose DOAC regimens: low-dose edoxaban in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48, the pooled low-dose regimens in the meta-analysis of the four pivotal trials, and 15 mg edoxaban in ELDERCARE-AF?

keyPoints.text: ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48: low-dose edoxaban was non-inferior to warfarin on stroke or systemic embolism (hazard ratio 1.07) with much less major bleeding (1.61% per year, hazard ratio 0.47); in the intention-to-treat analysis there was an unfavorable trend (hazard ratio 1.13).

support.quote: 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 1.07; 97.5% CI, 0.87 to 1.31; P=0.005 for noninferiority)
and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)
an unfavorable trend with low-dose edoxaban versus warfarin (hazard ratio, 1.13; 97.5% CI, 0.96 to 1.34; P=0.10)

keyPoints.text: The meta-analysis: low-dose DOAC regimens had overall stroke or systemic embolism similar to warfarin (RR 1.03) and a more favourable bleeding profile (RR 0.65), but significantly more ischaemic strokes (RR 1.28).

support.quote: Low-dose new oral anticoagulant regimens showed similar overall reductions in stroke or systemic embolic events to warfarin (1·03, 0·84-1·27; p=0·74), and a more favourable bleeding profile (0·65, 0·43-1·00; p=0·05), but significantly more ischaemic strokes (1·28, 1·02-1·60; p=0·045)

keyPoints.text: ELDERCARE-AF compared 15 mg edoxaban with placebo (not warfarin) in very elderly Japanese patients: stroke or systemic embolism was 2.3% vs 6.7% per year (hazard ratio 0.34), and the increase in major bleeding (3.3% vs 1.8% per year, hazard ratio 1.87) was not statistically significant (P=0.09).

support.quote: The annualized rate of stroke or systemic embolism was 2.3% in the edoxaban group and 6.7% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.34; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.19 to 0.61; P<0.001), and the annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.3% in the edoxaban group and 1.8% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.87; 95% CI, 0.90 to 3.89; P = 0.09)

keyPoints.text: ELDERCARE-AF also reported substantially more gastrointestinal bleeding events with edoxaban than with placebo.

support.quote: There were substantially more events of gastrointestinal bleeding in the edoxaban group than in the placebo group.

cases.prompt: Besides the head-to-head trials against warfarin in broad populations, what did AVERROES, ELDERCARE-AF and J-ROCKET AF show about stroke or systemic embolism and bleeding, and against which comparator or in which population was each done?

keyPoints.text: AVERROES compared apixaban with aspirin in patients unsuitable for vitamin K antagonists: stroke or systemic embolism was lower with apixaban (hazard ratio 0.45) without a significant increase in major bleeding (1.4% vs 1.2% per year, hazard ratio 1.13, P=0.57).

support.quote: There were 51 primary outcome events (1.6% per year) among patients assigned to apixaban and 113 (3.7% per year) among those assigned to aspirin (hazard ratio with apixaban, 0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.32 to 0.62; P<0.001)
There were 44 cases of major bleeding (1.4% per year) in the apixaban group and 39 (1.2% per year) in the aspirin group (hazard ratio with apixaban, 1.13; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.75; P=0.57)

keyPoints.text: ELDERCARE-AF compared 15 mg edoxaban with placebo in patients 80 years or older who were not candidates for standard-dose anticoagulation: stroke or systemic embolism was lower with edoxaban (hazard ratio 0.34) and major bleeding was not significantly higher (hazard ratio 1.87, P=0.09).

support.quote: compare a once-daily 15-mg dose of edoxaban with placebo in elderly Japanese patients (≥80 years of age) with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation who were not considered to be appropriate candidates for oral anticoagulant therapy at doses approved for stroke prevention

keyPoints.text: J-ROCKET AF compared a Japan-specific 15 mg rivaroxaban dose with warfarin in 1,280 Japanese patients: the principal safety outcome (major and non-major clinically relevant bleeding) was non-inferior (18.04% vs 16.42% per year, hazard ratio 1.11), intracranial haemorrhage was 0.8% vs 1.6%, and stroke or systemic embolism showed a strong trend toward reduction (hazard ratio 0.49, P=0.050).

support.quote: the rate of the principal safety outcome was 18.04% per year in rivaroxaban-treated patients and 16.42% per year in warfarin-treated patients (hazard ratio [HR] 1.11; 95% confidence interval 0.87-1.42; P<0.001 [non-inferiority]). Intracranial hemorrhage rates were 0.8% with rivaroxaban and 1.6% with warfarin.
There was a strong trend for a reduction in the rate of stroke/systemic embolism with rivaroxaban vs. warfarin (HR, 0.49; P=0.050).

cases.prompt: Across the four dedicated heart failure outcome trials of SGLT2 inhibitors (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced, EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER), how large was the reduction in the primary composite outcome in each, and does the effect hold across the ejection fraction range?

keyPoints.text: DAPA-HF (ejection fraction 40% or less): dapagliflozin reduced worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death, hazard ratio 0.74 (16.3% vs 21.2%).

keyPoints.text: EMPEROR-Reduced (ejection fraction 40% or less): empagliflozin reduced cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization, hazard ratio 0.75 (19.4% vs 24.7%).

keyPoints.text: EMPEROR-Preserved (ejection fraction above 40%): empagliflozin reduced the primary outcome, hazard ratio 0.79 (13.8% vs 17.1%).

support.quote: a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)

keyPoints.text: DELIVER (mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, above 40%): dapagliflozin reduced the primary outcome, hazard ratio 0.82 (16.4% vs 19.5%); results were similar for ejection fraction of 60% or more and less than 60%.
